author: cosmosarcive
name: Cosmos Archive
text:
Piezoelectricity began with a simple observation in 1880: squeeze certain crystals and they produce an electric charge. A year later, Gabriel Lippmann predicted the reverse, that an electric field should deform them, and the Curies confirmed it.

That two way conversion, mechanical energy to electricity and electricity to motion, is why the same physics now powers sensors, actuators and ultrasound.

author: cosmosarcive
name: Cosmos Archive
text:
Somewhere between a star and a black hole, the word “huge” stops being useful.

Earth is about 109 times smaller than the Sun. Stephenson 2-18 is estimated to span roughly 2,000 Suns, while TON 618 may contain about 41 billion solar masses. Its event horizon would be roughly 240 billion km across.

For a nonrotating black hole, the diameter is D = 4GM/c².

The universe does not just make bigger objects. It completely resets our sense of scale.

author: NextScience
name: Next Science
text:
🧠 Scientists Can Now Control Brain Cells With Light

What if scientists could switch specific brain cells on or off using tiny pulses of light?
That is the idea behind optogenetics—a powerful technology that has transformed neuroscience and earned the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel.

The story began with something surprisingly small: a single-celled green alga. Scientists wanted to understand how it detects light and moves toward it.

Hegemann and Nagel helped uncover channelrhodopsin, a light-sensitive protein that opens when exposed to blue light, allowing charged particles to cross the cell membrane.

Researchers then found a remarkable way to use this discovery in nerve cells.
